chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from Ahmad ibn Ali al-Katib from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Thaqafi from Abdullah ibn Abi Shaybah from Hariz from Ata ibn al-Sa'ib from Zadhan said:

Two men entrusted a trustworthy woman with a deposit and said to her, 'Do not give it to either of us until we meet at your place.' Then they left and were absent. One of them came to her and said, 'Give me my deposit, for my companion has died.' She refused until he disputed with her at length, then she gave it to him. Then the other came and said, 'Give me my deposit.' The woman said, 'Your companion took it and claimed that you had died.' They appealed to Umar, and Umar said to her, 'I do not see but that you have guaranteed it (liability).' The woman said, 'Make Ali (peace be upon him) judge between me and him.' Umar said, 'Judge between them.' Ali (peace be upon him) said, 'This deposit is with me, and you both commanded her not to give it to either of you until you both meet at her place. Bring me your companion, for he did not guarantee it.' And he said, 'They only wanted to take the woman's money.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a conditional deposit when one claimant says the other has died?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights Imam Ali’s judicial acumen in distinguishing between a simple deposit (*amanah*) and a guaranteed deposit (*daman*) based on the specific condition of mutual presence. By ruling that the first man’s unilateral removal of the deposit did not incur liability because the condition for release was not fulfilled, Ali demonstrated a precise application of contractual intent over literal possession. This case is frequently cited in Shia jurisprudence to illustrate the principle that conditions attached to trusts must be strictly observed to determine liability.
